column1: After weeks of posturing that it was preparing to call a strike by August 31, the Philadelphia Federation of Teachers abruptly rammed through a contract Thursday night. The move was intended to prevent a walkout by 14,000 educators in the nation’s eighth-largest school district.

According to the union’s own figures, less than half of the membership participated in the rushed online vote. Only 4,000 ballots were cast in favor—barely one quarter of the total membership—yet the PFT declared the agreement ratified.

This sham vote cannot be considered legitimate or binding by teachers. Philadelphia educators must organize themselves to override this sellout and prepare collective action independent of the union’s apparatus.

The agreement provides a 3 percent wage increase per year, a raise that does not keep pace with inflation in Philadelphia, which is already higher. At the same time, it introduces steep healthcare premium increases for new hires.

Paid interview time for kindergarten teachers has been eliminated under the contract. Even parental leave provisions will not take effect until next year, underscoring the regressive nature of the deal.

Over the summer, PFT members had voted by 94 percent to authorize a strike. The union even organized “strike ready” events with sign-making and rallies to project the image of preparing for confrontation.

The instant the PFT suddenly announced the tentative agreement, its tone changed by 180 degrees. From threatening to strike, the leadership shifted to celebrating a deal that promised “three years of labor peace.”

Philadelphia schools face a $300 million deficit, while the Southeastern Pennsylvania Transportation Authority is slashing services under “doomsday” cuts. These austerity measures mirror crises unfolding in every major urban district across the country.
PFT officials used intimidation and manipulation to present the contract as a fait accompli. Teachers reported being told that the union would not call a strike even if members rejected the deal.

The entire “strike ready” campaign was a maneuver to get in front of explosive rank-and-file anger. It functioned as a way to channel discontent back under bureaucratic control rather than unleash a genuine struggle.

Far from a sign of strength, such maneuvers reflect the profound weakness of the union apparatus. The leadership is terrified of the growing opposition from below, fueled by worsening living and working conditions.

This betrayal in Philadelphia follows the shutdown of the AFSCME municipal strike in July. That strike had disrupted July 4 festivities before being quickly suppressed in collaboration with the city’s Democratic mayor.

Teachers across the country are entering into struggle, pressing for strike action in California, Chicago, and New York. At the same time, both Democrats and Republicans are accelerating cuts to public education.

To wage a genuine fight, educators must form independent rank-and-file committees. Such bodies can override undemocratic decisions, assert control over bargaining, and organize strike action outside union control.

“With House and Senate Republicans still struggling to find consensus on a budget reconciliation bill extending and expanding Trump-era tax cuts, Representative Jason Smith made a surprising statement on May 4 about eliminating loopholes to help working-class Americans.”

“Smith said, ‘There’s no problem to eliminate loopholes that the wealthy have benefited from to make sure that working-class Americans aren’t paying taxes on tips, seniors are having reduced taxes on their Social Security, and we’re not paying taxes on overtime.’”
“Senior Trump administration officials remain interested in a variety of tax provisions, including potential rate increases for wealthy Americans, despite Trump’s past opposition to such hikes.”

“Whether Republicans will support higher taxes on the wealthy remains uncertain, with House Speaker Mike Johnson continuing to oppose them, while some populist figures like Vice President J.D. Vance back selective increases.”

“Smith’s framing is populist, designed to deflect Democratic criticism that GOP tax bills favor millionaires, echoing Steve Bannon’s advice that taxing the wealthy politically undercuts Democratic messaging.”

“A tax bill that increases taxes on the wealthy while reducing them for working-class households would resemble a Democratic approach more than a traditional Republican one, leaving Democrats without their usual critiques.”

“The distribution of benefits matters: eliminating taxes on tips, Social Security, and overtime primarily helps upper-middle-class households, with lower-income households gaining relatively little due to the progressive tax structure.”

“Estimates show that in 2026, removing Social Security taxes would give the bottom 20 percent $0, the next-lowest quintile $15, and the top one percent $2,205, with the top 0.1 percent getting $2,450.”
“Overtime and tip exemptions similarly favor higher earners: the bottom 20 percent might receive $10 (overtime) and $730 (tips), while the top 20 percent could see $1,480 and $7,170, respectively.”
“Trump’s regressive tariffs could offset any working-class gains from the tax changes, as consumer costs on goods increase regardless of income bracket.”
“Smith emphasized urgency, warning that failure to pass the bill could mean a 22 percent tax increase for all Americans, highlighting the political pressure to reach a compromise.”

“Negotiations remain fragile, balancing demands for severe spending cuts from fiscal hawks with swing-district political concerns, making the final impact on wealthy taxpayers dependent on the bill’s fine print.”

“The Democratic Party’s standing in public opinion polls has sunk to its lowest point in more than 30 years. Many of the party’s own voters think their leaders aren’t fighting hard enough against President Trump. In one survey, the words they used most often were ‘weak’ and ‘tepid.’”

“‘We’ve found our footing. We’ve gone on the offensive,’ argued Rep. Ro Khanna (D-Fremont), who spent most of the summer campaigning across the country. ‘Trump’s cuts to Medicaid and tax breaks for billionaires have given us a message we can unite around.’”

“‘The most important task of the Democratic Party is to organize … the most robust debate Democrats have had in a generation,’ said William A. Galston of the Brookings Institution, a former Clinton aide who argues that the party needs to move to the center.”

“Most Democrats also agree that they need to focus on a positive message on economic issues such as the cost of living — to use this year’s buzzword, ‘affordability.’ But they differ on the specifics.”

“Progressives like Sen. Bernie Sanders (I-Vt.) and Rep. Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez (D-N.Y.) have focused on ‘fighting oligarchy,’ including higher taxes on the wealthy and government-run health insurance.”

“A sharper debate has opened over social and cultural issues: Should Democrats break with the identity politics — the stuff Republicans deride as ‘woke’ — that animates much of their progressive wing? Moderate Democrats argue that ‘wokeness’ has alienated voters in the center and made it impossible to win presidential elections.”
“Pre-K-12 teachers made up 3.4% of the workforce in 2024, according to the Bureau of Labor Statistics. Demographically, teachers are more likely to be white, a woman, and in their 40s.”
“In 2022, teachers ages 30 to 49 made up over half the teaching workforce. Teachers in their 40s made up most of the teaching pool (26.1%), followed closely by those in their 30s at 25.4%.”
“Teachers in their 50s (20.4%) outnumbered those in their 20s (18.4%). Those 60 and older were 9.7% of teachers, the smallest age group.”

“In 2022, just over seven in 10 teachers (71.7%) were white. Hispanic teachers made up 11.6% of the workforce, and Black teachers were 9.4%. The remaining 7.3% included teachers of two or more races, Asians, and other groups.”

“White and multiracial teachers are represented disproportionately, comprising a larger share of the teaching workforce than of the general population. Hispanic, Black, Asian, Native American, and Pacific Islander teachers made up smaller shares.”

“As of 2024, around 70% of teachers in pre-K through secondary schools were white. Secondary schools had the biggest share of white teachers, with 86.2%. Black and Hispanic teachers were most represented in preschool and kindergarten.”

“White teachers made up a smaller share of educators in preschools and kindergartens (69.1%). Black teachers and Hispanic teachers were least represented in secondary schools, and Asian teachers in special education.”
“Among teachers working in elementary, middle, and high schools, annual pay varies by the grade level taught.”

“In 2022, nearly eight in 10 teachers at all levels—pre-K through 12th grade and special education—were women. Women are much more represented in education than in the workforce generally, where they were 46.8% that same year.”

“The share of male teachers increases as student age rises. At the earliest levels of education, preschool and kindergarten, 2.5% of teachers were men. This rose to nearly 20% in elementary and middle school, and just over 40% in secondary school.”

“Two attorneys who defended the Riverside County couple who made worldwide headlines after being accused of neglecting and abusing 12 of their 13 children are now heading up the defense of a different county couple who have received similar attention in a case in which the husband and wife are accused of killing their missing 7-month-old son.”

“In the Turpin case, Facebook groups sprang up in which followers of the drama — including many people from outside the United States — freely offered opinions about the couple’s culpability, David’s haircut and the children.”

“But amateur sleuths, armed with cell phone cameras, TikTok accounts and a love of juicy rumors with little appetite to confirm them, have taken the social media interest in the Haros and little Emmanuel to an exponentially higher level. Other posts hurl venom at the Haros.”
